title: Meta's Muse Personal AI Agent Launches in the UK
excerpt: Meta has rolled out its Muse personal AI agent to users in the United Kingdom. Launched in the U.S. in September, Muse can complete tasks for users...
content_html:
Tuesday November 24, 2026 3:15 am PST by Tim Hardwick

Meta has rolled out its Muse personal AI agent to users in the United Kingdom. Launched in the U.S. in September, Muse can complete tasks for users on their behalf, like sending an email or booking travel.


The yeti-like character Meta designed to represent Muse appears in its standalone app, and users can also interact with the agent via WhatsApp.

Meta says Muse is a tool users can trust to lend a "helping hand" with anything, from chasing a refund to doing the Christmas shopping. Muse can also use payment credentials at checkout with Link, a secure wallet for agents built by Stripe.

From the press release:

With Muse, you're in control. You choose what it can access, approve important actions before Muse carries them out , and can ask it to remember and or forget something. We built Muse to be private, safe, and secure by design. Every Muse gets its own virtual computer in the cloud, like a laptop that's just for you. Your information and logins are kept there, not in Meta's other services, and no one else's Muse can access them.

Meta says Muse is launching in the U.K. with popular global Connectors, and it also partners with British brands and retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, ASOS, Currys, easyJet and Jet2. Muse can only be used by people aged 18 and over.

Muse has been downloaded more than 10 million times in the U.S., but it's had a bit of a fraught start despite its popularity. Reuters reported last week that Meta staffers had raised concerns internally about "undesired actions" carried out by the agent since it went live, from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases. Meta has called these "isolated incidents."

OpenAI in September also launched a rival personal AI agent collectively called "Dots," but it has yet to roll out to the UK market.
